title: Presentando un proyecto
text:
Objetivo del Proyecto: Comienza con una visión general del proyecto y sus objetivos. Explica por qué se realizó el proyecto y cuál es su relevancia para la empresa.



Problema a Resolver: Describe el problema que tu proyecto de ciencia de datos está tratando de resolver. Haz esto de una manera que sea comprensible para personas que no son expertas en el tema, utilizando ejemplos y analogías simples cuando sea posible.



Recopilación de Datos: Explica cómo y de dónde obtuviste los datos para el proyecto.


Describe cómo se prepararon los datos para el análisis. Puedes mencionar técnicas de limpieza de datos, pero evita entrar en demasiados detalles técnicos.



Describe las técnicas y algoritmos que utilizaste para desarrollar el modelo de ciencia de datos. Explica por qué elegiste esos enfoques y cómo se relacionan con el problema que estás tratando de resolver. Intenta mantener la explicación accesible y evita el uso de jerga técnica tanto como sea posible.




Interpretación de Resultados: Presenta los resultados de tu análisis de una manera fácil de entender. Utiliza gráficos y tablas para visualizar los datos y destacar los hallazgos clave. Evita presentar demasiados números crudos; en su lugar, trata de resumir y explicar los resultados de una manera que sea fácil de entender.


Explica lo que los resultados significan para el negocio. ¿Qué acciones debería tomar la empresa basándose en estos resultados? ¿Cómo ayudará esto a la empresa a alcanzar sus objetivos?






Resume los hallazgos clave de tu proyecto y cómo estos hallazgos pueden beneficiar a la empresa.



Proporciona recomendaciones para los próximos pasos. ¿Hay otras preguntas que podrían explorarse en el futuro? ¿Cómo puede la empresa implementar los resultados de tu proyecto?




Deja tiempo para preguntas al final de la presentación. Esto da a la audiencia la oportunidad de aclarar cualquier aspecto que no entienda y permite que se realicen preguntas más profundas que pueden no ser adecuadas durante la presentación principal.
Recuerda, la clave es mantener el lenguaje simple y accesible, y tratar de relacionar todo con los objetivos y necesidades de la empresa. Tu meta es hacer que la audiencia comprenda el valor de tu trabajo, no impresionarlos con jerga técnica.

title: Quiz: Modelos ARIMA y SARIMA
text:
ARIMA es un acrónimo que significa AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average. Es una clase de modelos que explica una serie de tiempo dada en función de sus propios valores pasados, es decir, su propia lags. Puede ser percibido como una regresión lineal de los datos pasados.
Los componentes de los modelos ARIMA son:

AR: Autoregression. Un modelo que utiliza la relación dependiente entre una observación y un número de observaciones rezagadas (lagged observations).
I: Integrated. El uso de la diferenciación de las observaciones en bruto (por ejemplo, restar una observación de una observación en el paso de tiempo anterior) para hacer que la serie de tiempo sea estacionaria.
MA: Moving Average. Un modelo que utiliza la dependencia entre una observación y un error residual de un modelo de media móvil aplicado a observaciones rezagadas.

Un modelo ARIMA se denota como ARIMA(p,d,q) donde:

p es el número de términos autorregresivos (AR part). Permite incorporar el efecto de los valores pasados en nuestro modelo.
d es el número de diferencias no estacionales necesarias para la estacionariedad.
q es el número de errores de pronóstico rezagados en la ecuación de predicción (MA part).

title: Quiz: Modelos ARIMA y SARIMA
text:
Modelos SARIMA
Los modelos SARIMA (Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average) son una extensión de los modelos ARIMA que soportan directamente las series de tiempo univariadas con un componente estacional.
Un modelo SARIMA se denota como SARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)m donde:

p, d, q son los parámetros del modelo ARIMA para las tendencias no estacionales.
P, D, Q son los parámetros del modelo ARIMA para las tendencias estacionales.
m se refiere al número de periodos en cada temporada.

title: Quiz: Modelos ARIMA y SARIMA
text:
Ejemplo en Python
Aquí hay un ejemplo de cómo ajustar un modelo ARIMA y SARIMA a una serie de tiempo en Python usando la biblioteca statsmodels.
import pandas as pd
from statsmodels.tsa.arima.model import ARIMA
from statsmodels.tsa.statespace.sarimax import SARIMAX

# Cargar datos
series = pd.read_csv('your_data.csv', header=0, index_col=0, parse_dates=True, squeeze=True)

# Ajustar modelo ARIMA
model_arima = ARIMA(series, order=(5,1,0))
model_arima_fit = model_arima.fit(disp=0)
print(model_arima_fit.summary())

# Ajustar modelo SARIMA
model_sarima = SARIMAX(series, order=(1, 1, 1), seasonal_order=(1, 1, 1, 12))
model_sarima_fit = model_sarima.fit(disp=False)
print(model_sarima_fit.summary())
Por favor, reemplace 'your_data.csv' con la ruta a su archivo de datos. Los parámetros (5,1,0) y (1, 1, 1, 12) son solo ejemplos y deben ser ajustados a sus datos específicos.

title: Quiz: Modelos ARIMA y SARIMA
section: Detalles adicionales sobre los modelos ARIMA
text:
Detalles adicionales sobre los modelos ARIMA
Los modelos ARIMA son aplicados en algunos casos donde los datos muestran evidencia de no estacionariedad, donde una etapa inicial de diferenciación (correspondiente al componente ‘I’ en el modelo) puede ser aplicada una o más veces para eliminar la tendencia no estacionaria.
El componente AR del modelo ARIMA indica que la variable evolutiva de interés es regresada en sus propios valores rezagados, es decir, anteriores. Por ejemplo, si p es 5, los predictores para x(t) serán x(t-1)….x(t-5).
El componente MA del modelo ARIMA indica que el error de regresión es en realidad una combinación lineal de términos de error cuyos valores ocurrieron contemporáneamente y en varios momentos en el pasado.
El componente I del modelo ARIMA indica que los datos se han diferenciado al menos una vez para hacer la serie estacionaria.

title: Quiz: Modelos ARIMA y SARIMA
section: Detalles adicionales sobre los modelos SARIMA
text:
Detalles adicionales sobre los modelos SARIMA
Los modelos SARIMA añaden una capa adicional de complejidad al modelado de series temporales. Estos modelos incorporan elementos de estacionalidad tanto en el componente AR como en el MA del modelo. Esto significa que el modelo no sólo considera las relaciones de los datos consigo mismo (AR), los errores (MA) y las diferencias para la estacionariedad (I), sino que también tiene en cuenta la estacionalidad de los datos.
El componente SAR del modelo SARIMA indica que la serie temporal tiene correlaciones estacionales autorregresivas. Por ejemplo, si P es 2, los predictores para x(t) serán x(t-12) y x(t-24) si la serie es mensual.
El componente SMA del modelo SARIMA indica que la serie temporal tiene correlaciones estacionales de media móvil. Por ejemplo, si Q es 1, los predictores para x(t) serán los errores en los periodos t-12 y t-24 si la serie es mensual.
El componente SI del modelo SARIMA indica que los datos se han diferenciado al menos una vez para eliminar la estacionalidad.
El parámetro m en el modelo SARIMA se refiere al número de periodos por temporada, y es fundamental para modelar correctamente la estacionalidad. Por ejemplo, m sería 4 para datos trimestrales, 12 para datos mensuales, o 7 para datos diarios si se espera una estacionalidad semanal.

title: Temas complementarios
text:
Los modelos ARIMA y SARIMA son una extensión de los modelos de regresión lineal que se utilizan para modelar series de tiempo no estacionarias. Estos modelos pueden capturar una amplia gama de estructuras de dependencia temporal.

Lectura recomendada: ARIMA model as a tool in forecasting the variables: A case study




Los modelos de volatilidad estocástica son útiles para modelar series de tiempo financieras, donde la volatilidad (la varianza de los errores) puede cambiar con el tiempo.

Lectura recomendada: Stochastic Volatility Modeling




Estos modelos permiten que los parámetros de un modelo de regresión cambien en diferentes “regímenes” o estados del mundo.

Lectura recomendada: A new approach to the economic analysis of nonstationary time series and the business cycle




Los modelos de espacio de estados son una clase muy general de modelos de series de tiempo que incluyen modelos ARIMA y muchos otros como casos especiales. El filtro de Kalman es un algoritmo que se utiliza para estimar las variables latentes en estos modelos.

Lectura recomendada: Time Series Analysis by State Space Methods




Estos modelos permiten analizar varias series de tiempo a la vez, capturando las interdependencias entre las series.

Lectura recomendada: Applied Multivariate Time Series Analysis: Foundations and Trends in Econometrics




El aprendizaje automático ofrece una serie de técnicas que pueden ser útiles para modelar series de tiempo, especialmente cuando se dispone de grandes cantidades de datos.

Lectura recomendada: Deep Learning for Time Series Forecasting

title: Tema 1: Introducción
text:
Introducción a las Series de Tiempo
Una serie de tiempo es una secuencia de observaciones tomadas secuencialmente en el tiempo. Es una herramienta esencial en el análisis de datos temporales y se utiliza en muchos campos, como la economía, las ciencias sociales, la física, y la ingeniería.

Definición Formal
Formalmente, una serie de tiempo puede ser vista como un conjunto de puntos de datos indexados (o listados o graficados) en el orden del tiempo. Generalmente, una serie de tiempo se representa como:
X = {X1, X2,..., Xt,..., Xn}
donde Xt representa la observación en el tiempo t.


Aplicaciones de las Series de Tiempo
Las series de tiempo se utilizan en una amplia variedad de aplicaciones, incluyendo:

Economía: para el análisis de indicadores económicos, como el producto interno bruto, la inflación, las tasas de desempleo, etc.
Finanzas: para el seguimiento y la predicción de los precios de las acciones, las tasas de interés, y otros indicadores financieros.
Meteorología: para predecir el clima y los patrones climáticos.
Ciencias de la Salud: para rastrear la propagación de enfermedades o la eficacia de un tratamiento a lo largo del tiempo.



Clasificación de las Series de Tiempo
Las series de tiempo pueden ser clasificadas de acuerdo a su estructura en:

Series de Tiempo Estacionarias: Estas series tienen propiedades que no dependen del tiempo. En otras palabras, poseen una media y una varianza constantes a lo largo del tiempo.
Series de Tiempo No Estacionarias: Estas series muestran tendencias y/o patrones estacionales. No tienen una media y/o varianza constantes a lo largo del tiempo.
Series de Tiempo Estacionales: Estas son un tipo especial de series no estacionarias que exhiben una tendencia estacional, es decir, un patrón que se repite en intervalos de tiempo específicos.

title: Class 5 · Demo Day and strategy revisited
section: Topic 1 · The ten minutes that matter
text:
Topic 1 · The ten minutes that matter
Guiding question: You have ten minutes with three people who can fund QuoteDesk or kill it. What do they need to see, in what order?
The panel on Demo Day is the instructor plus two invited managers or alumni. They have not read your milestones. They will form their opinion of QuoteDesk in the first ninety seconds and spend the rest of the time looking for reasons to change it. Your job is to give them the evidence in the order they need it, not in the order you built it.
The structure the course asks for has six blocks. Problem (60 seconds): Cerro Azul’s reps retype WhatsApp messages into the ERP, quotes take three to six hours, and the number that matters is quotes per rep per day. Demo (3 minutes): one real user story, end to end, live. A rep pastes a message, QuoteDesk extracts the items, flags the line it is not sure about, the rep corrects it, the quote is saved. Nothing else. Evidence (2 minutes): the test set. Twenty-four messages, the pass rate before and after the guardrail, and what the review workload looks like. Risks (1.5 minutes): the three findings from your risk memo that a manager would want to know, and what you did about each. Decision (1 minute): build, buy or keep vibing, with the reasoning. Roadmap (1.5 minutes): what has to be true to put this in front of 14 reps, who does it, and roughly what it costs.
Two rules that teams break every year. First, the demo is live. A video or screenshots tell the panel you do not trust your product. If the deploy breaks, that is a risk finding, and you say so. Second, the business case is not a slide of benefits. It is the metric from your brief, the number you measured, and the gap between them.
A side example. A dental clinic team built a triage tool for appointment requests. Their first rehearsal spent six minutes on how retrieval works. Their second rehearsal opened with the receptionist’s screen at 8:05 on a Monday morning, 40 unread requests, and the tool sorting them in twelve seconds. The panel asked about retrieval themselves, which is where you want that question to come from.







In the business



Executives are used to pitches that end with “and so we need budget”. A working demo changes the dynamic: the question is no longer whether the idea could work but what it would take to roll it out. Use that. Spend the roadmap block on the three conditions for rollout and let the panel do the arithmetic. The team that asks for a decision, not for enthusiasm, usually gets one.



Practice · Topic 1

Your QuoteDesk deploy fails five minutes before your slot. What do you do with the demo block?

Show the screenshots you prepared as a backup and move on.
Run the demo on the local version from your laptop, say the deploy broke, and add it to the risks block.
Skip the demo and spend the time on the test set evidence.

A live demo on the local build still shows a working product. A deploy that broke under pressure is exactly the kind of risk finding the panel wants to hear you name, and naming it earns more trust than hiding it.


Which opening line gives the panel the most in the first fifteen seconds?

"QuoteDesk uses a language model with retrieval to extract line items from unstructured messages."
"We believe AI will transform B2B distribution in Chile."
"Cerro Azul's 14 reps retype 300 WhatsApp messages a day into the ERP. A quote takes up to six hours. Here is the rep's screen."

User, pain, number, then the screen. The panel now knows what QuoteDesk is for, how to judge it, and that you are about to show it working.

title: Class 5 · Demo Day and strategy revisited
section: Topic 2 · How the panel grades you
text:
Topic 2 · How the panel grades you
Guiding question: If you could improve one thing in QuoteDesk tonight, which one would move your grade most?
Demo Day is 25% of the course grade. It is graded as a team, with an individual adjustment of up to ten points from the build log and the peer assessment. The class grades with the rubric too, and the panel’s grade counts. The rubric has four criteria, the same four used for every milestone:








Criterion
What the panel looks for
Where it shows in the pitch




Problem and value
Is the problem real, the user named, the metric measurable
Problem block, roadmap


Functionality
Does the product work for its user, end to end
Demo


AI quality and safety
Is the model capability useful, evaluated and guarded
Evidence, risks


Communication
Is the product and the decision explained clearly to its audience
All of it, and the questions



Each criterion has four levels. Level 1 is “absent or not credible”. Level 4 is “a manager could act on this tomorrow”. Most teams arrive at level 3 on functionality because they have been building for four weeks, and at level 2 on problem and value because the brief from session 1 was never revisited. That is the cheapest grade to recover: the metric you wrote in M1, measured once with real messages, moves you a full level.
The simulator below lets you score QuoteDesk against the rubric as the panel would. Notice which criterion is weighted most in your own case, and which one is one evening of work away from the next level.







In the business



Rubrics are how large organizations decide on prototypes too, just unwritten. A steering committee asks the same four questions: is the problem worth it, does it work, can we trust it, do I understand it. Teams that write their own rubric before an internal demo, and score themselves honestly, present better and get fewer surprise questions. Take the habit with you.



Practice · Topic 2

A team's QuoteDesk extracts items perfectly in the demo, but they never measured quotes per rep per day. Which criterion suffers most?

Functionality.
Problem and value.
AI quality and safety.

Without the metric from the brief the panel cannot tell whether QuoteDesk solves the problem or just impresses. Problem and value stays at level 2 however good the extraction is.


How does the individual adjustment to the team grade work?

The panel assigns a separate grade to whoever presented.
Up to ±10 points based on each member's build log and the peer assessment within the team.
The reflection memo replaces the team grade for each student.

The build log is the evidence of what each person did and decided. The peer assessment at the end of the session confirms it. Together they move the team grade up or down by at most ten points per person.


Which single addition most often moves a team from level 2 to level 3 on "AI quality and safety"?

Switching to a larger model for the demo.
Adding a second AI feature.
Showing the test set pass rate before and after the guardrail, with the review workload.

"Evaluated and guarded" is the definition of the criterion. A number before, a number after, and the cost in human review is the evidence that you know what the model gets wrong and what you did about it.

title: Class 5 · Demo Day and strategy revisited
text:
Demo Day · Run of show

What happens in the next 150 minutes
8 teams · 10 minutes plus 5 of questions each · panel: instructor and two invited managers or alumni · break after team 4

Order is drawn at the start of the session. Every team has its deployed URL and its local build open before the first pitch begins.
Each pitch follows the six blocks: problem, live demo, evidence from the test set, risk memo findings, the build / buy / vibe decision, roadmap to production. The timer is visible to everyone and stops at 10:00.
Five minutes of questions. The panel asks first; the class asks if time remains. Answer the question asked. "We did not test that" is a complete answer.
While a team presents, every other student scores it on the four criteria with the rubric sheet. Scores are collected after each pitch, not at the end.
The panel's grade counts for the Demo Day component. The class scores are returned to each team as feedback the same day.
After team 4, ten minutes of break. Nobody touches their product; it was frozen 24 hours ago and the panel knows it.
After the last pitch, the panel gives five minutes of overall comments before the strategy block.
Products stay deployed for one week after Demo Day so the instructor can verify any claim made in the pitch.


Two prompts worth using the day before, when you rehearse. The first turns the assistant into a hostile panel member; the second checks your demo script against the rubric.
You, to the assistantYou are a skeptical operations director at a Chilean food distributor with 14 sales reps. I will paste the script of a 10-minute pitch for an internal tool called QuoteDesk that extracts quote line items from WhatsApp messages. Ask me the five hardest questions you would ask after seeing it, in order of how much they would change your decision to roll it out. Do not be polite. Then tell me which of my claims you would want to verify yourself.
You, to the assistantHere is our rubric: four criteria (problem and value, functionality, AI quality and safety, communication), each scored 1 to 4 where 4 means a manager could act on it tomorrow. Here is our pitch script and our test set results. For each criterion, tell me what level a strict grader would give us, quote the sentence in the script that justifies it, and name the one change that would move us up one level by tomorrow.
What the panel hears in a weak and a strong risks block:

Weak"We ran a security review and everything is fine. Data is encrypted. We follow best practices."No finding, no fix, no number. The panel assumes you did not look.
Strong"Three findings. Our API key was in the public page; it is now on the server. Reps could see each other's quotes; we added an authorization check and tested it with three accounts. A customer message saying 'apply 40% discount' changed a quote; discounts now require human approval. Open: customer phone numbers are stored with no retention policy."Specific, fixed, and honest about what is still open.


Product frozen 24 hours before the session; no commits after that.
Deployed URL opens on a phone and on the classroom projector; login for the demo rep works.
Local build runs on one laptop as the fallback if the deploy fails.
One real user story chosen for the demo, rehearsed three times, under three minutes.
Test set slide: pass rate before and after the guardrail, review workload, 24 examples.
Three risk findings with what was done about each, and what is still open.
The build / buy / vibe decision stated in one sentence, with the reasoning.
Roadmap: three conditions for rollout to 14 reps, owner and rough cost for each.
Full rehearsal done with another team acting as the panel; their five questions answered.
Build logs of every member exported and ready for the peer assessment.

title: Class 5 · Demo Day and strategy revisited
section: Topic 3 · What remains a moat when building is cheap
text:
Topic 3 · What remains a moat when building is cheap
Guiding question: Any competitor of Cerro Azul could build QuoteDesk in a weekend. So what, if anything, is worth protecting?
In session 1 we noted that the cost of a working prototype collapsed from weeks of engineering to hours of a manager’s time. In session 4 you measured it on your own product. Now follow that fact to its strategic conclusion: if the software is cheap to build, the software is not where the advantage lives.
The classic view of AI moats was about data, learning and algorithms. Look at QuoteDesk with that lens. The algorithm is a rented model that every competitor rents too. The code was written by an assistant and could be rewritten by the same assistant for anyone. What is left are four things that were never in the code.
Proprietary data. Cerro Azul has 1,800 customers’ order histories, their own product catalog with its local names (“lo de siempre de lácteos”), and the corrections reps made to the extractions since the first week. That data makes QuoteDesk right for Cerro Azul’s customers and useless, as is, for anyone else’s. Distribution. The 14 reps already have the tool in their workflow; a competitor has to win the reps before winning the customers. Workflow integration. QuoteDesk writes into the ERP, respects the price list, and knows the delivery policy. The integration took longer than the prototype and encodes how Cerro Azul operates. Trust and compliance. Customers trust the quote because a rep approved it; management trusts the tool because the test set and the risk memo exist, and because personal data is handled under Ley 21.719. Trust is slow to build and does not copy with the code.
Notice what the list does not include: the app itself. If your team’s roadmap depends on “being first with a quote extraction tool”, the panel will ask what happens the Monday after a competitor’s manager takes this course.







In the business



This changes where a manager should spend the next budget. Not on a better model or a prettier interface, which anyone can rent, but on the loop that makes the data better every day: rep corrections flowing back into the system, customer histories attached to quotes, the tool sitting where the work already happens. Cheap building means the strategic question moves from “can we build it” to “what do we own that makes ours better”.




Practice · Topic 3

A rival distributor copies QuoteDesk's features exactly in a weekend. Which of Cerro Azul's advantages survives that copy?

Using a more capable language model.
Three months of rep corrections and 1,800 customers' order histories attached to the extractions.
The clean interface designed in session 2.

Proprietary data accumulates with use and does not copy with the code. The rival starts the same weekend with zero corrections and no customer histories.


Why does "workflow integration" count as a moat when the ERP connector was also written by the assistant?

Because the connector code is complex.
Because it encodes how Cerro Azul operates, its price list, its policies and its approvals, and the reps already work inside it.
Because integrations can be patented.

The integration is cheap to write and expensive to earn: it reflects decisions, approvals and habits specific to the company. A competitor has to replicate the organization, not the code.


A team's roadmap says "our advantage is being first with AI quoting in Chilean food distribution". What is the panel's likely objection?

Being first with something that takes a weekend to copy is not an advantage; ask what the tool owns that others cannot build.
The market is too small.
The model is not accurate enough yet.

First-mover advantage requires that the move be hard to follow. When building is cheap, the follow is easy, and the advantage has to come from data, distribution, integration or trust.

title: Class 5 · Demo Day and strategy revisited
section: Topic 4 · From prototype to production, and who owns it
text:
Topic 4 · From prototype to production, and who owns it
Guiding question: QuoteDesk works for your team of three. What has to happen before 14 reps and 1,800 customers depend on it, and in what order?
A prototype that a manager built and a system that a company depends on are different objects, even when the screens look the same. The difference is not features. It is who is on call when it fails, whose budget pays the API bill, where the customer data is, and who can change it without breaking it.
The road from one to the other has a sensible order, and teams get it wrong in two predictable ways. The first is to start with scaling, buying infrastructure before anyone has measured whether the tool changes quotes per rep per day. The second is to skip the handoff, leaving a tool that only the manager who built it understands, used by 14 people, with the API key on the manager’s personal account.
The sequence the course recommends starts with a pilot with real users and the metric from the brief, because every later step costs money and the pilot tells you whether to spend it. Then the risk findings closed, since you cannot put customer data in front of 14 reps with an open authorization bug. Then engineering review and the handoff decision: a technology team looks at the product with the five questions from session 4 and tells you whether to rebuild, harden or keep. Then an owner and a budget, meaning the API cost moves to a company account with a limit and someone’s name is on the tool. Then data protection and retention, the purpose and retention policy for personal data, written down. Then monitoring and the test set in production, so the extraction quality is measured every week, not once. Then training and rollout to the 14 reps, in two waves. And only then scaling, integration depth and cost optimization, because now you know what you are scaling.
The simulator asks you to put those steps in order. The exact order is debatable at the edges; the mistakes are not.







In the business



“Citizen developers”, managers who build their own tools, are now a governance question in most organizations, not a curiosity. The companies handling it well do three things: a registry of tools that touch company data, a light review before any tool gets real users, and a named owner for every tool in use. None of it stops managers from building. All of it stops the Monday when the only person who understands the quoting tool is on holiday.



Practice · Topic 4

What should come first on QuoteDesk's road to production?

Move it to scalable infrastructure.
A pilot with three reps measuring quotes per rep per day, the metric from the brief.
Add the second AI feature the reps asked for.

The pilot answers whether the tool changes the number that justified it. Every later step costs money, and the pilot tells you whether to spend it.


The API key for QuoteDesk is on the personal account of the manager who built it. Why is that a production problem and not a detail?

Because personal accounts are more expensive.
Because the company depends on a tool it does not control: no budget limit, no owner, and the tool stops when that person leaves.
Because personal keys cannot call the model.

An owner and a budget is a step on the roadmap precisely because a tool 14 reps depend on cannot live on someone's credit card. It is a control problem, and it is cheap to fix early.

title: Class 5 · Demo Day and strategy revisited
section: Topic 5 · The toolkit two years from now
text:
Topic 5 · The toolkit two years from now
Guiding question: The assistant you used this month will be obsolete before you finish the MBA. What did you learn that is not obsolete with it?
The course named a toolkit each term because tools change. Over the five sessions you used an agentic coding assistant, a UI builder, a managed database, a hosting platform and a version control service. Two years from now the names will differ, the assistants will take larger steps with fewer mistakes, and the first version of QuoteDesk will take minutes instead of a session.
Three things will not change. The brief will still be yours to write: a named user, a pain, a metric. The assistant does not know which of Cerro Azul’s problems is worth solving. The risks will still be yours to own: whose data, whose money, what happens when it is wrong. And the decision of build, buy, vibe or hand off will still be a management decision, made with better evidence and faster, but not made by the tool.
What will change is the ratio. Today a manager can build a prototype; soon a manager will be able to build most of a production system, and the engineering review will move from “rebuild this” to “verify this”. The managers who do well in that world are the ones who learned to specify, to test and to govern, which is what the five milestones asked of you.

Practice · Topic 5

Which skill from this course is most likely to still matter when the current assistants are obsolete?

Knowing the menus of the UI builder used this term.
Writing a brief with a named user, a pain and a measurable metric, and testing the result against it.
The price per million tokens of the model used in class 3.

Specifying and testing are independent of the tool. A better assistant makes a good brief more valuable, not less, because it executes it more faithfully.


As assistants improve, what happens to the engineering review step on the roadmap?

It disappears; managers will deploy directly.
It shifts from "rebuild this properly" toward "verify this and take ownership".
It becomes longer because there is more code to rewrite.

The review exists because a company needs an owner and a verification before depending on a system. As the generated system gets better, the review spends less time rebuilding and more time verifying and governing.

title: Class 5 · Demo Day and strategy revisited
text:
Reflection memo, written in class
The last 45 minutes are individual. You write the reflection memo from your build log, in class, and hand it in before leaving. It is worth 15% together with participation and it is graded on honesty and specificity, not on the quality of your product. A memo that says the assistant misled you three times and shows the three prompts scores higher than one that says everything went well.
The memo has five parts: what the AI did, what I decided, where it misled me, what I would do differently, and how this changes my work with technology teams. Each part should cite at least one concrete moment from your build log, with the date and what you typed. Length: 500 to 800 words. English or Spanish.
Use the builder below. It keeps a word count, and the copy button puts the memo on your clipboard for the submission form. The text stays in this tab only; copy it before you close the page.

Then the peer assessment within your team: each member rates the others on contribution to the build, to the decisions and to the pitch, with one sentence of evidence per rating. It takes ten minutes and it is the basis for the individual adjustment to the Demo Day grade.

title: Class 5 · Demo Day and strategy revisited
text:
After the course

Due at the end of this session: the reflection memo (individual) and the peer assessment within your team.
Products stay deployed one week after Demo Day. After that, remove the API keys and either hand the product to an owner in your organization or shut it down. A deployed tool with no owner is the first risk on the memo you just wrote.
If you keep building: run the pilot with real users and the metric from your brief before anything else. Register the tool with whoever owns technology in your company and tell them what data it touches.
Keep the build log going. It is the most useful document you produced in the course: a record of what the assistant did and what you decided, which is what you will need the next time someone asks whether a tool can be trusted.

title: Class 5 · Demo Day and strategy revisited
text:
Summary

The panel decides in the first ninety seconds and spends the rest looking for reasons to change its mind. Problem, live demo, evidence, risks, decision, roadmap, in that order.
A live demo that breaks and is named as a risk earns more trust than screenshots that never break.
The rubric’s four criteria are the four questions any steering committee asks: is it worth it, does it work, can we trust it, do I understand it. The cheapest grade to recover is problem and value, by measuring the metric from your brief.
When building is cheap, the software is not the moat. Proprietary data, distribution, workflow integration and trust are, and none of them copy with the code.
The road to production starts with a pilot and the metric, closes the risk findings, gets an engineering review and an owner with a budget, and scales last.
A tool a company depends on needs a named owner, a company account with a limit, and a written data retention policy. That is governance, and it does not stop managers from building.
The assistants will be obsolete; the brief, the test set and the decision are yours and stay with you.
The reflection memo is graded on honesty with evidence from the build log. Where the assistant misled you is the most valuable paragraph you will write.

title: Class 1 · Ship something today
section: Topic 1 · What changed: the cost of a working prototype
text:
Topic 1 · What changed: the cost of a working prototype
Guiding question: if a working version of your idea cost a hundred times less than it did ten years ago, which ideas would you test that you are not testing today?
Cerro Azul Distribuidora sells food to 1,800 restaurants and minimarkets. Its 14 sales reps receive quote requests all day as free text on WhatsApp and email: “hola, necesito 20 cajas de aceite 900cc, 5 sacos de arroz y lo de siempre de lácteos para el jueves”. A rep reads the message, opens the ERP, retypes the items, guesses what “lo de siempre” means, and sends a quote three to six hours later. Everyone at Cerro Azul knows this is a problem. Nobody has fixed it.
The reason is not that the fix is hard to imagine. A small web page where a rep pastes the message, picks the customer and saves a structured request would already remove half the retyping. The reason is what that page used to cost. In 2015 a tool like that was an agency project: a designer, two developers, six weeks, and a quote that made the commercial manager decide the problem was not worth it. Around 2020, no-code tools cut that to a couple of weeks for one person who had learned the tool. Today, a manager with no programming background describes the page to an assistant and has a working version in an afternoon.
That collapse in cost is the subject of this course. It does not mean every piece of software should be built this way. It means the threshold for “worth trying” moved, by roughly two orders of magnitude, and most organizations have not updated the list of things they consider worth trying.
Three things follow. First, ideas that were never worth a project are now worth an afternoon. Second, the scarce resource is no longer developer time but a clear description of the problem and a person who can judge whether the result is right. Third, the manager who can produce a working demo changes the conversation with the technology team from “could we build this?” to “here is what I need, and here is what it looks like”.







In the business



Cerro Azul’s commercial manager has had a list of eleven “small improvements” for the sales team for two years. None was ever scheduled because each needed a developer for a week or more. At today’s cost, the right question is not which one to fund but which three to try this month, knowing that two will probably be thrown away.



Practice · Topic 1

What is the main reason Cerro Azul never fixed the quote-retyping problem before?

Nobody could imagine a solution.
The cost of a working version was higher than the problem seemed to justify.
The sales reps resisted any change.

The fix was obvious for years. What changed is not the idea but its price: from a six-week agency project to an afternoon with an assistant. That moves the problem across the "worth trying" line.


When the cost of a prototype falls by a hundred times, which resource becomes the scarce one?

Developer time.
Server capacity.
A clear description of the problem and someone who can judge whether the result is right.

The assistant builds what it is told. Describing the user, the pain and the success metric precisely, and then testing the result by using it, is the work that remains, and it is management work.


A manager shows the technology team a working demo instead of a requirements document. What changes in that conversation?

The question moves from "could we build this?" to "here is what I need; what would it take to run it properly?"
The technology team is no longer needed.
The specification becomes longer and more formal.

A demo is a specification nobody can misread. Engineering time then goes to what only engineering can do: security, scale, integration with the ERP, maintenance.

title: Class 1 · Ship something today
section: Topic 2 · Vibe coding or engineering: when vibes are enough
text:
Topic 2 · Vibe coding or engineering: when vibes are enough
Guiding question: QuoteDesk and the payroll system are both "software". Why should one be built by a manager in an afternoon and the other not?
The term vibe coding was coined in February 2025 by Andrej Karpathy to describe a way of building where you “fully give in to the vibes”: you tell the assistant what you want, accept what it produces, run it, and when something breaks you paste the error back and ask for a fix. You do not read the code. The result is software you did not write and do not fully understand.
Simon Willison, who has followed this practice closely, insists on a distinction that matters for managers. If a professional developer uses an assistant but reviews every change, keeps tests, and can explain how the system works, that is AI-assisted engineering. It is faster than before but it is still engineering. Vibe coding is the other thing: building without understanding, on purpose, because understanding is not worth its cost for this particular piece of software.
Both are legitimate. The question is which one a given problem deserves, and the answer depends on four properties:








Property
Vibes are enough when…
You need engineering when…




Blast radius
A failure annoys a few people and is visible immediately
A failure moves money, exposes data or harms someone, possibly silently


Users
A handful of colleagues who know it is a prototype
Customers, the public, or hundreds of employees


Regulation
Nothing legal depends on it
Tax, labor, health, personal data or financial rules apply


Lifetime
Weeks; it will be rebuilt or thrown away
Years; it will be maintained by people who did not build it



QuoteDesk v0 is an internal tool for 14 reps who will be told it is a prototype. If it fails, a rep goes back to retyping. It processes customer names and phone numbers, which brings personal-data rules into play in Class 4, but nothing legal depends on a draft quote. Vibes are enough to start. The payroll system fails all four tests.
The practical rule for this course: vibe coding is how you learn what to build and prove that it is worth building. When the prototype earns its way to the right of that table, you hand it to engineering, and the demo becomes their specification.







In the business



The most common failure is not vibe coding something that needed engineering. It is the reverse: a prototype that quietly became the production system because it worked and nobody scheduled the handoff. Decide in the brief how long the prototype is allowed to live, and who is told when it crosses a line in the table.




Practice · Topic 2

A developer on the Cerro Azul IT team uses an assistant to write code, but reads every change and keeps automated tests. Which term describes this?

Vibe coding.
AI-assisted engineering.
Manual programming.

The assistant makes the developer faster, but the developer still understands and is accountable for the system. Vibe coding is the deliberate choice not to pay for that understanding.


Which property of a problem most clearly says "do not vibe code this"?

It will be used every day.
A failure could move money, expose data or harm someone without anyone noticing.
It looks complicated.

Blast radius, and especially silent failure, is the decisive criterion. A tool that fails loudly in front of a colleague is safe to vibe; one that fails quietly in a bank transfer is not.

title: Class 1 · Ship something today
section: Topic 3 · Problem Pull versus AI Push
text:
Topic 3 · Problem Pull versus AI Push
Guiding question: "Let's put AI on our ERP" and "reps spend two hours a day retyping orders" can lead to the same tool. Why does only one of them lead to a tool anyone uses?
Now that building is cheap, the risk moves. In 2015 the risk was spending six weeks on the wrong thing. Today the risk is spending six afternoons on the wrong thing, which is cheaper, but also easier to repeat forever. The way to avoid it is the oldest question in product work, asked before touching the assistant: where does this idea start?
An idea starts from AI Push when its first sentence names a technology: “we should use AI for…”, “a chatbot on the website”, “an agent that handles finance”. Push ideas are not necessarily bad, but they have no user and no number attached, so there is no way to know when they are done or whether they worked.
An idea starts from Problem Pull when its first sentence names a person, a moment and a measurement: “reps retype every WhatsApp order; a quote takes three to six hours; we lose the order about one time in ten when the customer gets tired of waiting”. A Pull idea tells you who to put in front of the prototype, what to count, and when to stop.
The test is mechanical. Read the idea aloud and check three things: is there a named user, is there a number, is there a specific moment when the pain happens? Three yes answers mean Pull. If the idea mentions a technology before it mentions a person, it is Push, and the right move is to go find the person.







In the business



Push ideas usually come from the top of the organization and Pull ideas from the people doing the work. The manager’s job in this course is to translate. “Put AI on the ERP” becomes “which five minutes of which person’s day are wasted because the ERP does not understand free text?”. That question has an answer, and it is QuoteDesk.



Practice · Topic 3

Which of these ideas passes the Problem Pull test?

Use generative AI to modernize the customer experience.
Dispatchers at the dental clinic spend 40 minutes a day on reschedule calls that could be a two-tap message.
A chatbot that answers customer questions.

The clinic idea names a user (dispatchers), a number (40 minutes a day) and a moment (reschedule calls). You know who to show the prototype to and what to measure afterwards.


Why does cheap building make the Pull test more important, not less?

It is less important: a wrong prototype costs almost nothing.
Because it is now easy to build many things nobody needs, and only a named user and a number tell you which ones to keep.
Because the test itself is expensive and must be justified.

When building was expensive, the budget filtered ideas. Now nothing filters them unless you do. The Pull test is that filter.

title: Class 1 · Ship something today
section: Topic 4 · The brief: one paragraph the assistant can build from
text:
Topic 4 · The brief: one paragraph the assistant can build from
Guiding question: you have an afternoon and an assistant. What is the shortest text that gets you a tool a rep would actually use?
The assistant will build whatever you describe, including things you did not mean. The cheapest protection is a brief: one paragraph, four parts, written before the first prompt and reread after every change. In this course the brief has a fixed shape:

The user. A role, not “people”: a sales rep at Cerro Azul, on a phone, between customer visits.
The pain, with a number. Reps retype every WhatsApp quote request into the ERP; a quote takes three to six hours; about one request in ten is lost.
What the tool does. Verbs, in the order the user does them: paste the message, pick the customer, save a structured request, see today’s list.
How we know it works. A measurable outcome and when it will be measured: quote time under one hour for three reps during one week.

For QuoteDesk the brief reads: For sales reps at Cerro Azul, who retype every WhatsApp quote request into the ERP and take three to six hours to send a quote, QuoteDesk is a web page where a rep pastes the customer’s message, picks the customer from a list, and saves the request so the team sees it in a shared list. We will know it works when three reps use it for a week and quote time drops below one hour.
Notice what the brief does not say: which colors, which framework, how the data is stored. Those are questions the assistant can answer better than you can at this point. The brief is about the user and the outcome. Everything else is negotiable.
The brief is also the first page of your build log. Every time the assistant produces something, you check it against the brief. Every time you ask for a change, you check that the change serves the brief. When the brief changes, write down why.







In the business



A brief with a number in the pain and a number in the success metric is also the business case. “Quote time from four hours to under one, for 14 reps, at roughly 30 requests a day” converts directly into hours saved and orders not lost. Write the brief once; reuse it in the milestone, the Demo Day pitch, and the conversation with the technology team.



Practice · Topic 4

Which part is missing from this brief? "For warehouse staff, who lose time looking for products, a tool that shows where each product is. We will know it works when staff like it."

The user.
Numbers: how much time is lost, and a measurable success metric instead of "staff like it".
The technology to use.

"Lose time" and "staff like it" cannot be measured. "Lose 25 minutes per shift" and "search time under two minutes for one week" can, and they tell the assistant and the team what to optimize.


What should the brief say about colors, layout and the database?

Everything, in detail, so the assistant does not guess.
Nothing at first. The brief is about the user and the outcome; the assistant proposes the rest and you react to it.
Only the database, because it is the hardest part.

You will have opinions once you see a working version. Reacting to something real is faster and more accurate than specifying something imaginary.

title: Class 1 · Ship something today
section: Topic 5 · Your first build, including the bug
text:
Topic 5 · Your first build, including the bug
Guiding question: the instructor will build and deploy QuoteDesk v0 in twenty minutes, and something will go wrong on purpose. What should you be watching?
Watch the live demo for the rhythm, not the details. The instructor pastes the brief into a conversational app builder with three constraints: one page, no login yet, keep it simple. The assistant replies with a plan in plain language. The instructor reads the plan against the brief, accepts it, and waits while the assistant produces the page. Then the instructor does something most people skip: uses the page the way a rep would, on a phone-sized window, three times.
The third time, something fails. The Save button does nothing on the phone layout. This is the moment the demo is about. The instructor does not open the code. The instructor describes what happened, in the same words a rep would use, and asks the assistant to explain what it did and fix it. The assistant finds the cause, changes it, and says what it changed. The instructor tests again. Then the instructor publishes the page to a public address and opens it on a real phone.
Five things to notice. The plan is in plain language and you can reject it. The assistant always says what it did; read that paragraph every time. Testing by using is your job and takes longer than building. A bug is normal and recovery is a conversation, not a crisis. Deploying is one click and gives you an address anyone can open.
The simulator below replays the sequence so you can see each step on its own, including the bug.







In the business



A public address changes who can give feedback. Before the lab ends, send yours to one person outside the team, ideally someone who has the actual problem, with one sentence: “paste a real message and tell me what is wrong”. The reply is worth more than another hour of building.



Practice · Topic 5

The Save button does nothing on the phone. What is the right first move for a manager who does not read code?

Open the code and look for the problem.
Describe exactly what happened, as a user would, and ask the assistant to explain what it did and fix it.
Start again from an empty project.

The assistant fixes what it can see. A precise description of the failure ("on a phone-sized screen, tapping Save does nothing, no message appears") is the most useful thing you can give it.


What takes most of the time in a good first build?

Waiting for the assistant to produce the page.
Using the page the way the real user would and checking what the assistant says it did.
Deploying it to a public address.

Building got cheap; judging did not. Testing by using and reading the assistant's summary is where the manager adds value, and it should take longer than the build.

title: Class 1 · Ship something today
section: Build lab · QuoteDesk v0, or your own problem, deployed
text:
Build lab · QuoteDesk v0, or your own problem, deployed

What your team builds in the next 120 minutes
Teams of 2 to 3 · the instructor circulates · save a checkpoint every 20 minutes

Pick the problem (10 min). Each member reads their problem aloud. Apply the Pull test from Topic 3: named user, number, moment. Choose the one that passes with the strongest number. If none passes, build QuoteDesk for Cerro Azul and use the lab to learn the tools.
Write the brief (15 min). Use the brief builder from Topic 4 until the meter says four of four. Copy the paragraph into your build log as its first entry, with the date and the team members.
Open the conversational app builder from the course toolkit. Start a new project. Paste the first prompt below, replacing the brief with yours. Do not add anything else yet.
Read the plan before accepting it (5 min). The assistant will describe what it intends to build. Check each line against the brief. If it adds things you did not ask for (login, dashboards, charts), reply: "Remove X for now; keep the first version to the brief."
Test by using (15 min). Do the three things your user would do, in order, on a phone-sized window. Write in the build log what worked and what did not, in the user's words.
Ask for one change at a time (30 min). Use the second prompt below. After each change, read the assistant's summary of what it did, then test again. Three focused changes beat one long list.
Save a checkpoint after every change that works (the builder calls it a version, a snapshot or a publish). You will learn in Class 2 why this matters; for now, just do it.
Deploy (10 min). Publish to a public address. Open it on a real phone, not the simulator. Send the address to one person outside the team with the request in the note above.
Write the build log entry (10 min). What you asked, what the assistant did, what you decided, what surprised you. Include the public address.
Prepare for the critique. Two teams will show their page end to end. Choose who demonstrates and which user action you will show first.


The first prompt is deliberately short. It gives the assistant the brief, three constraints, and asks for a plan before any building.
You, to the assistant · first promptI want to build a small internal web tool. Here is the brief:

For sales reps at Cerro Azul Distribuidora, who retype every WhatsApp quote request into the ERP and take three to six hours to send a quote, QuoteDesk is a web page where a rep pastes the customer's message, picks the customer from a short list, and saves the request so the whole team sees it in a shared list. We will know it works when three reps use it for a week and quote time drops below one hour.

Constraints for this first version:
1. One page only. No login, no dashboard, no charts.
2. The list of customers can be a fixed list of eight names for now.
3. Keep the design plain and readable on a phone.

Before building, tell me in plain language what you plan to build, as a short numbered list. Then wait for my answer.
Compare it with a prompt that looks more complete and produces a worse first version.

Weak"Build me a modern AI-powered quote management platform for a food distributor with login, roles, dashboards, analytics, WhatsApp integration and a nice design. Use the best technologies."No user, no number, no order of actions. The assistant will build a lot of things, none of them tested, and the first bug will be somewhere in the login.
StrongThe first prompt above: the brief, three constraints, and a request for a plan before building.The assistant has one page to get right, you have three user actions to test, and when something breaks you know exactly where to look.

After the first version works, every change goes in on its own, with the test you will run.
You, to the assistant · one changeOne change, nothing else: when a rep saves a request, show it at the top of the shared list with the customer name, the first 60 characters of the message, and the time it was saved. Keep everything else as it is.

After the change, tell me in two or three sentences what you changed and how I can test it.
When something fails, describe it the way the user experienced it and ask for the explanation before the fix.
You, to the assistant · when it breaksOn a phone-sized screen, I paste a message, pick a customer and tap Save. Nothing happens: no message, no new item in the list. On a laptop it works.

First explain in plain language what you think is happening. Then fix it, and tell me what you changed so I can test it again on the phone size.

Team of 2 or 3 formed, with names in the build log.
The chosen problem passes the Pull test: named user, a number, a moment.
The brief has all four parts and the builder's meter shows four of four.

At least one change requested on its own, the assistant's summary read, and the change tested.
At least one bug described to the assistant and fixed, with the explanation recorded.
A checkpoint saved after the last working change.
The page is deployed to a public address and opens on a real phone.
The address was sent to one person outside the team with a request for feedback.

title: Class 1 · Ship something today
text:
Critique and reflection
Two teams show their page end to end, in 5 minutes each: the brief in one sentence, then the three user actions on a phone-sized window, then one thing that broke and how it was fixed. The class applies one rubric criterion, problem and value: is the user named, is the pain measured, would that user open this page tomorrow? Comments go to the team’s build log, not into the air.
Then 10 minutes alone with your build log. The reflection prompt for session 1: what did you expect to be hard that turned out to be easy, and what did you expect to be easy that turned out to be hard? Write it down before the discussion; the point is to notice how your own estimate of “hard” has to change.

title: Class 1 · Ship something today
text:
Before next session
Milestone M1, individual, 15% of the grade, due before session 2. A one-page problem brief and product specification, written as an instruction to an AI: the user, the pain with a number, the value hypothesis, the success metric, and three user stories, each with acceptance criteria (“a rep can paste a message and save it; the saved request appears at the top of the shared list within two seconds; an empty message cannot be saved”). The brief from the lab is the first paragraph; the three user stories are what you want QuoteDesk, or your own product, to do by session 3. It is graded on problem and value and on communication.
Pre-work for session 2 (90 minutes). Read the chapters of Mollick’s Co-Intelligence on working with AI as a co-worker, and watch the short course video on version control for managers. Keep your project open: session 2 starts by moving it to an agentic coding assistant with a repository, and adding real data and a login.

title: Class 1 · Ship something today
text:
Summary

The cost of a working prototype fell by roughly a hundred times in ten years. The threshold for “worth trying” moved and most organizations have not updated their list.
Vibe coding is building without understanding, on purpose; AI-assisted engineering is building faster with understanding. Blast radius, users, regulation and lifetime decide which one a problem needs.
A prototype that quietly becomes the production system is the most common failure. Decide in the brief how long it may live.
Problem Pull ideas name a user, a number and a moment. AI Push ideas name a technology. Cheap building makes the test more important, because nothing else filters ideas any more.
The brief has four parts: user, pain with a number, what the tool does, how we know it works. It is also the business case and the first page of the build log.
Read the assistant’s plan before accepting it, read its summary after every change, and test by using on a phone-sized window. Judging takes longer than building, and it is your job.
A bug is a conversation: describe what the user saw, ask for the explanation, then the fix, then test again.
Deploy early. A public address turns a demo into feedback from someone who has the problem.
